ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA (operator-set, Day 23, DEV.102 — measurable, not aspirational): (1) the six known flakes CLASSIFIED timing-vs-state, each with evidence; (2) e2e completes UNDER 15 MINUTES with ZERO retries; (3) no spec skipped, disabled, `fixme`-d, or given a longer timeout to get there. Criterion 3 exists so criterion 2 cannot be met by weakening what is tested. NOTE: `globalTimeout` was raised 20 → 40 min on Day 23 (DEV.102) on its own merits and gives F.52 room to work, but does NOT satisfy criterion 2 — that is measured against actual runtime, not against the cap. DAY 24 PHASE 1 — verify-day-6 CONFIRMED FLAKY ON MAIN, and its signature BREAKS the characterisation above. Post-merge run 34309474851 on main (commit 664cca8 — the run this baseline is read from): 65 tests, 1 worker, 64 passed / 1 flaky / 0 failed, suite 18.5 min, e2e job 19m38s, whole run 22m15s. Against the acceptance criteria that is a FAIL on both halves of criterion 2 — 18.5 min against a sub-15-min target, and one retry against a zero-retry target. The flake was `verify-day-6.spec.ts:45:7 > Day 6 — inventory + procurements > procurement detail page renders for a seeded procurement`, failing at line 54 on `await expect(page.locator("h1")).toContainText(/PROC-/)` — a 15 s CONTENT assertion, NOT a navigation or visibility timeout. verify-day-6 was ALREADY one of the known-flaky six, so this adds evidence rather than a seventh spec; what is new is that the claim above — "all timeouts on navigation/visibility, none an assertion that data was wrong" — no longer holds for the set. Treat that sentence as superseded for verify-day-6. CLASSIFICATION IS GENUINELY OPEN; DO NOT CARRY A GUESS INTO THE TRIAGE. The first read on the day was "state bug — the seeded procurement is not visible to the query". That read is wrong on the evidence, and the operator said why: a state bug of that shape re-runs the SAME query against the SAME database on the retry and fails again. It passed on retry. That is more consistent with the content not being RENDERED yet than with it not EXISTING. But neither reading is to be assumed. A late h1 has a timing explanation (first-hit dev-server route compile, 5-10 s, DEV.87 — the same mechanism part (1) of this task targets) AND a state explanation (a row becoming visible only after an earlier spec commits), and the observable is identical either way. This is precisely what N=5 against a virgin database is for: run flake-triager on verify-day-6, fresh DB, 5 runs, and let the per-run evidence classify it. Criterion 1 requires evidence, not a plausible story. SECOND OBSERVATION — PR #5 (docs-only branch docs/dev-103-merge-gate), run 34327213279, e2e job 102387759938: 63 passed / 2 flaky / 0 failed, suite 17.8 min. Both flakes were known-set specs: verify-day-19.spec.ts:183 (operator impersonation, toHaveURL — the DEV.93/DEV.101 signature) and verify-day-6.spec.ts:45 — the SAME toContainText(/PROC-/) failure at line 54 as the baseline run, again passing on retry. verify-day-6 has now flaked on two consecutive runs, on two different branches, the second from a docs-only diff that touched no spec, no app route and no schema. THE TWO OBSERVATIONS ARE NOT INDEPENDENT, AND THE CLASSIFICATION STAYS OPEN. Both runs execute the same 65 specs in the same order on a single worker, so a state bug seeded by an EARLIER spec's write would clear on the retry in both runs exactly as observed. The repetition raises the reproduction RATE; it does not raise confidence in either classification. What two reproductions do buy is triage economics — verify-day-6 is the cheapest spec in the set to get a verdict on, because it actually reproduces. Runtime for the two runs was 18.5 min and 17.8 min, both with retries burning time, so the gap to criterion 2 is a consistent ~3-4 min structural gap rather than run-to-run noise. TRIAGE ORDER (Day 24 Phase 1, operator-set) — supersedes the listing order of the six above, which was arbitrary: (1) verify-day-6 — two reproductions in two runs on different branches, the strongest signal in the set; (2) verify-day-19 — two reproductions (DEV.101 on PR #3, and PR #5), same toHaveURL signature both times; (3) verify-day-c2 — one reproduction, Day 22 post-merge run 34126383303; (4) verify-day-5; (5) verify-day-16 (accessibility); (6) verify-day-c1 — LAST, and deliberately so. c1 has not reproduced since DEV.93: five escalating local repros against a virgin DB failed to reproduce it, and it passed on CI run 2 with no fix applied. It may cost N runs to tell us nothing, so it is not where the first budget goes. This inverts the old order, in which c1 led because it was the first flake seen, not because it was the most tractable. The ordering of (2)-(5) was not operator-specified: it is by reproduction count, then by whether the failure has a recorded signature. Reorder freely if a run changes the evidence. CLOSED Day 24. BOTH acceptance criteria met, and the day's own theory of the cause was wrong. CRITERION 2 MET ON CI: PR #6, run 34391508643 — `65 passed (9.3m)`, ZERO flaky, ZERO failed, e2e job 11m58s (was 17m40s on run 34375881563). ROOT CAUSE was NOT first-hit route compilation. It was Next dev ON-DEMAND-ENTRIES EVICTION: `pagesBufferLength: 5` and `maxInactiveAge: 60s` against a suite that visits ~40 routes over a 16-19 minute run, so almost every route was evicted and recompiled repeatedly — measured locally `/login` 5x, `/dashboard` 5x, `/dealers/[id]` 4x, and on CI run 34375881563 `/dealers` and `/dealers/[id]` 3x each with module counts VARYING between compiles (5464 -> 4307 -> 4429), which is eviction and rebuild, not a server restart. Each recompile costs 8-16s on CI and lands on whichever test touches the route next, against a 15s expect budget. FIX = two coupled changes: `onDemandEntries` in apps/web/next.config.mjs (dev-only keys; `next build` ignores them, so it cannot reach production — a deliberate scope call recorded in DEV.105) plus the mandated route warm-up pass in apps/web/tests/e2e/global-setup.ts. MEASURED BEFORE KEEPING, workers:1, virgin DB each run: baseline 18.8min (63 passed/1 flaky/1 FAILED); warm-up ONLY 21.3min (62 passed/2 flaky/1 FAILED) — the mandated fix SHIPPED ALONE MADE THE SUITE SLOWER, because eviction discarded it; onDemandEntries only 9.4min then 9.3min on repeat (65 passed, 0 flaky); BOTH 6.9min (65 passed, 0 flaky). The warm-up was kept only because it then earned its place: in the final configuration ALL compilation completes during warm-up and ZERO compiles occur during the test phase, versus 44 still landing inside test budgets without it. Confirmed on CI: 17 compiles total, 0 after `Running 65 tests`, 0 restarts, one server lifetime. CRITERION 3 HELD: no spec skipped, disabled, fixme-d or given a longer timeout. Three specs had a `page.setDefaultTimeout` BELOW the config default with no stated reason (verify-day-c1:54, operator-onboarding:72 at 15s; verify-day-19:186 at 30s) — REMOVED, not raised; operator-onboarding failed on exactly that 15s budget in the baseline run and got further on retry. The two overrides that DO carry a stated reason (operator-readonly-view:31, critical-path:140) were left alone. CRITERION 1 — the six classified: verify-day-6 TIMING FLAKE with the mechanism established positively by flake-triager (the click is an RSC SOFT navigation, so `page.locator('h1')` keeps resolving the LIST page's `

` until the transition commits; 19 resolutions across 15s is a compile longer than the expect budget; there is no prefetch in dev so the click is the route's first hit); verify-day-19 TIMING FLAKE, three reproductions all on :183 `toHaveURL`, including one local pre-fix (attempt 0 failed 89.5s, attempt 1 PASSED 7.3s — retry got further, the DEV.93 signature); verify-day-c1 / operator-onboarding TIMING FLAKE, reproduced locally pre-fix with the retry getting further (attempt 0 `page.goto` 15000ms, attempt 1 `page.waitForURL` 15000ms one step later); verify-day-c2 TIMING FLAKE on CI run 34126383303, `toHaveURL` on /dealers/[id] at 15s, passed on retry. verify-day-5 and verify-day-16: NOT REPRODUCED, N=5 each, and BOTH triagers independently reported that their place on the list rests on nothing substantiable — no CI reproduction, and no failure in any of six full-suite runs on Day 24. DELISTING THEM IS AN OPEN OPERATOR DECISION, deliberately not taken here. IMPORTANT CAVEAT, do not let it be lost: the local `verify-day-6` failures on Day 24 were `ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED` from a dev-server memory restart (DEV.106), which is a DIFFERENT failure mode from CI's `toContainText(/PROC-/)` — the local instrument was reproducing a local environment fault, not the CI flake, and every post-fix NOT REPRODUCED verdict was taken under warmed, non-evicting, raised-heap conditions and says nothing about pre-fix behaviour. CONFIDENCE, STATED HONESTLY: runtime and compile counts are solid (five full-suite runs, two of the same configuration agreeing within 4 seconds, plus CI). Flake ELIMINATION is not proven — three consecutive clean runs is three runs. The claim is that the mechanism is understood and removed, not that the suite has been observed stable long enough. DEV.104 (globalTimeout inversion), DEV.105 (eviction + scope call), DEV.106 (local-only memory restart), DEV.107 (agents proven, resolves DEV.96), DEV.108 (parallelism NOT raised). RECLASSIFIED Day 24 follow-up: verify-day-5 and verify-day-16 are NOT delisted from the known-flaky six — delisting would imply they were fixed, and they were never demonstrated broken. They are moved to an explicit WATCH — NEVER EVIDENCED state, tracked as F.62. See F.62 for the reasoning and for what a future appearance of either should be treated as. Also corrected: this task's completedDate was 2026-09-09 (session start) and is now 2026-09-10, the date of commit e373a8d which actually marked it complete. RUNTIME WATCH, opened by the operator after the PR #7 merge: e2e came in at 10m7s on the final PR #7 run (CI run 34498478642, suite `65 passed (9.1m)`), against 9.4-9.5m on the three runs before it. One observation, still comfortably inside the 15-minute acceptance criterion and inside the 25-minute globalTimeout, and not a regression on any evidence available — but it is the FIRST run above ten minutes since the fix landed, so 9.5m should not be assumed to be the steady state. WHAT TO WATCH, and why it is not obviously noise: the job wall-clock and the suite's own reported time can move independently, because the job also carries ~1 min of install/browser-install/migrate/seed plus the ~100-120s route warm-up in global-setup.ts, and the warm-up's own cost varies with GitHub runner CPU (measured 106.0s, 119.1s, 119.1s across three runs). So a rising job time with a flat suite time means the warm-up or the setup got slower, while a rising SUITE time would mean compilation has started leaking back into the test phase — which is the thing F.52 actually fixed and the only one of the two that would matter. The diagnostic that separates them is already in the logs and costs nothing: count `Compiled /` lines occurring AFTER `Running 65 tests` in the e2e job. The fix's signature is ZERO (confirmed on runs 34391508643 and 34426329250: 17 compiles total, all during warm-up, none during the test phase). A non-zero count on a future run means on-demand-entries eviction has returned — check that `onDemandEntries` is still present in apps/web/next.config.mjs and that nothing has raised the route count past `pagesBufferLength: 100`. Do NOT respond to a slow run by raising a timeout; that is the failure mode criterion 3 exists to prevent. RUNTIME WATCH CLOSED by the operator after six post-fix CI runs. THE STEADY STATE IS A BAND, NOT A POINT: 9.1-9.7 min of suite time (runs 34391508643, 34426329250, 34492261635, 34498478642, 34569838273, 34581641886), with job wall-clock 10m7s-11m58s. Treat 9.1-9.7 as the band and do NOT treat 9.5 as a point estimate — the earlier 10m7s observation that opened this watch was inside normal variance, not a regression, and the variance lives in the job rather than the suite (the warm-up's own cost has measured 106.0s / 119.1s / 119.1s / 121.7s with runner CPU). THE SIGNATURE HELD ON EVERY RUN CHECKED: zero `Compiled /` lines after `Running 65 tests`, zero dev-server restarts, one server lifetime. STOP TRACKING THIS. Resume only on one of exactly two signals, which are the two that would mean on-demand-entries eviction has returned: (1) a run exceeding 11 MINUTES of suite time, or (2) ANY `Compiled /` line appearing after `Running 65 tests` in the e2e job log. Either one means check that `onDemandEntries` is still present in apps/web/next.config.mjs and that the route count has not grown past `pagesBufferLength: 100`. Neither signal is a timeout problem and neither is to be answered by raising a timeout — that is the failure mode criterion 3 exists to prevent. Routine run-to-run jitter inside the band is not a signal and should not be investigated.

tasks.task: Make PROJECT_PLAN.md ENTIRELY generated — move the narrative out, so no hand-editable region remains (folded into F.37)
tasks.notes: Opened by the Day 24 follow-up, on `verifier`'s recommendation (DEV.113). THE PROBLEM: `PROJECT_PLAN.md` carries Stage 0 and Stages A-E, plus all headings, OUTSIDE the `STAGE_F_TASKS` markers. `.claude/agents/verifier.md` now says no change outside the markers is permitted, full stop. But `.claude/settings.json` denies `Edit`/`Write` on the file, CLAUDE.md §10.4 says it is 'never hand-edited, by any agent, ever', and `pnpm plan:sync` only writes between the markers. So the file is simultaneously REQUIRED to change eventually and UNCHANGEABLE by any approved route. A Stage G heading, a stage retitle, a typo fix in a Stage A row, or the A-E restructure implied by F.37 and F.56-F.60 are all legitimate and all currently forbidden. WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS: left alone, the DEV.112 situation recurs verbatim — correct verifier FAIL, operator overrule, another unsatisfiability entry — until overrule becomes routine and CLAUDE.md §10.3 erodes. That erosion is exactly what DEV.112 worked hardest to prevent, so this task is the defence of that entry, not a retreat from it. VERIFIER'S RECOMMENDATION, on record in its Day 24 report and NOT yet adopted: separate the invariant that actually matters — generated content is never hand-edited, and `plan:sync` never clobbers authored content — from its current over-approximation, which is 'nothing outside the markers may change'. Make an out-of-marker edit SATISFIABLE BUT EXPENSIVE AND VISIBLE rather than forbidden: its own commit, touching only `PROJECT_PLAN.md`, a conventional token in the commit message, and a DEVIATIONS entry referencing it; the verifier then checks every out-of-marker changed line belongs to a so-tagged commit and that the entry exists. Tighten the complement so it is not a loophole — inside such a commit the generated region must be byte-identical, and the `## Changelog` ban stays absolute and independently enforced by scripts/sync-project-plan.test.ts. The §10.4 / settings.json inconsistency must be fixed in the SAME change or the rule amendment is dead on arrival: scope §10.4 to 'the generated block is never hand-edited' and give the operator a recorded path while keeping the agent-level Edit/Write denial. EXPLICITLY REJECTED by the verifier, do not reach for it: 'allow out-of-marker changes when the operator approves' — that is the precedent DEV.112 refused to set and it reduces the rule to a formality. LONGER-RUN ALTERNATIVE, noted and not recommended next: bring the whole document under `plan:sync` so no out-of-marker region exists and the rule is trivially satisfiable forever — cleaner end state, more work, and it makes the historical A-E tables JSON-editable, which carries its own review cost. THIS IS A DECISION-BEARING CHANGE to a gate's pass condition and to CLAUDE.md: main-thread work per §10.4, and the operator's call per §10.1. Not urgent today; certain to bite. DECIDED BY THE OPERATOR, Day 24 follow-up: ELIMINATE THE HYBRID. Do NOT sanction a permitted-edit path. The reasoning, recorded because it is the part worth keeping: a permitted-edit path reintroduces exactly the drift the deny exists to prevent, and routine overrule turns CLAUDE.md §10.3 into a formality. DEV.112 also OVERCLAIMED — its 'exactly one commit in this repository's history must fail this check' is false going forward, because ANY legitimate out-of-marker change fails the rule, and the queued docs work already contains one: POST_PILOT_WORK_ORDER.md §1.5 wants PROJECT_PLAN.md updated to record that Stage E never completed and that UMA is on hold. That is a real, legitimate, currently-impossible edit, not a hypothetical. THE SHAPE OF THE FIX: (1) move the narrative — Stage 0, Stages A-E, and Risks & Open Items — into a normally-editable file (docs/PROJECT_HISTORY.md or similar), where ordinary editing rules apply and no deny rule is needed at all; (2) `scripts/sync-project-plan.ts` renders the WHOLE of PROJECT_PLAN.md from `docs/stage-f-tasks.json` plus a small committed header template; (3) the verifier rule becomes 'no hand edits at all' rather than 'none outside the markers' — trivially satisfiable forever, with no out-of-marker region left to argue about; (4) the `Edit`/`Write` deny in `.claude/settings.json` becomes unqualified and CORRECT rather than a blunt instrument with a known dead zone; (5) the Changelog guard's form-specificity stops mattering — `not.toMatch(/^##\s+Changelog\s*$/m)` would not catch `### Changelog` or `## Changelog — restored`, and a fully generated file cannot acquire a section by hand, so the gap closes structurally rather than by widening the regex. FOLDED INTO F.37, same PR: F.37 is already moving build history into docs/archive/ with `git mv`, so this is the same shape of work on the same files at the same time. Doing it separately would mean two restructures of the same documents. HONEST COST, stated rather than buried: roughly a day, and `sync-project-plan.ts` ends up owning more than the Stage F task table — it becomes the renderer for the whole document, which is more surface in one script. That is smaller than living with a file that structurally cannot be maintained. SUPERSEDES the 'VERIFIER'S RECOMMENDATION, not yet adopted' paragraph above: that recommendation was to make an out-of-marker edit satisfiable-but-expensive, and the operator rejected it for the reason given at the top of this decision. The verifier's own 'longer-run alternative' — bring the whole document under plan:sync — is what was chosen. Its one stated objection to that, that it makes the historical A-E tables JSON-editable, is answered by moving the narrative to a plain markdown file instead of into JSON. THIRD INSTANCE, and the operator's judgement is that it is the SHARPEST of the three: `PROJECT_PLAN.md:3` still reads 'Append a dated entry to the changelog at the bottom every time you mark something done.' The `## Changelog` section it refers to was deleted on Day 24 (DEV.110), so line 3 is now a STANDING WRITTEN INSTRUCTION TO PERFORM THE FORBIDDEN EDIT — the edit CLAUDE.md §10.4 forbids, `.claude/settings.json` denies, and the verifier's containment check fails. WHAT MAKES IT THE SHARPEST: line 3 sits OUTSIDE the `STAGE_F_TASKS` markers, so correcting the instruction is ITSELF blocked by the rule the instruction violates. The document cannot be brought into a consistent state from inside its own rules. That is not a rule with a gap — it is the argument for the fix. A sed to correct line 3 was offered to the operator on Day 24 and deliberately not applied by the main thread, because applying it would have required exactly the out-of-marker hand edit under discussion. HOW FULL GENERATION RESOLVES IT, BY CONSTRUCTION RATHER THAN BY CORRECTION: once `PROJECT_PLAN.md` is rendered in its entirety, line 3 becomes part of the committed header template, so it is PRODUCED correctly on every sync rather than needing to be fixed in place. There is no edit to authorise, no exception to carve, and no stale instruction to remember to chase — the inconsistency cannot exist in a generated file because the generator is the only thing that writes the line. Note this also means the header template must be written with line 3 already corrected: do not port the current text across verbatim, or the fix ships the defect it was meant to remove. The three known instances to check against the finished template are (1) POST_PILOT_WORK_ORDER.md §1.5's request to record that Stage E never completed and UMA is on hold, (2) the Stage 0 / Stage A-E / Risks narrative itself, and (3) this line 3 instruction. REQUIRED CHANGE, NOT INCIDENTAL — operator instruction, Day 24 follow-up. As part of this task, `outsideMarkers()` in `scripts/sync-project-plan.ts` MUST have its NUL sentinel replaced with any non-NUL value. Treat this as acceptance criteria for F.63, not as a nice-to-have discovered along the way. THE REASON IT IS CALLED OUT HERE: this task otherwise reads as being about MOVING NARRATIVE SECTIONS out of PROJECT_PLAN.md, and a one-line sentinel change inside a helper function is exactly the kind of item that gets dropped when the work turns out to be bigger than expected. It is recorded in F.65 and in DEV.117/DEV.118 as well, but F.65 is an audit task that may be scheduled separately or closed on its own, so relying on it to carry this change is how the change gets lost. WHAT AND WHY: the sentinel is a literal NUL at offset 9441 / line 264 — `return \`${plan.slice(0, pos.start)}\0${plan.slice(pos.end + MARKER_END.length)}\`` — and it is the reason search tools classify this file as binary. The Claude Code `grep` shim (ugrep) then exits 1 with NO OUTPUT on it, a silent false negative; `rg -n` lists no lines without `-a`; GNU grep prints `binary file matches`. The sentinel's PURPOSE is sound and must be preserved: it stands in for the generated block so that comparing outside-markers before and after proves the script touched nothing else, and `verifier` uses exactly that as its strongest containment evidence. ANY non-NUL value works, because the string is only ever compared against ITSELF, before versus after — a printable improbable token, or `\u0001`. Do not remove the sentinel; replace the byte. NOTE THE INTERACTION WITH THIS TASK'S OWN SHAPE: F.63 makes PROJECT_PLAN.md entirely generated, which means `outsideMarkers()` may cease to have a meaningful out-of-marker region to compute at all, and the function may be removed or reshaped rather than merely edited. That is fine and is the better outcome — but if the function survives in any form, the NUL must not. Verify after the change by confirming a plain `grep -c MARKER_START scripts/sync-project-plan.ts` returns 4 with exit 0 rather than exiting 1 with no output, and that `verifier`'s containment check still produces its byte comparison. ACCEPTANCE CRITERION ADDED BY THE OPERATOR 2026-09-14, stated as a GENERAL RULE because there are now two instances of the same trap. EVERY DANGLING OR WRONG ID IN THE MIGRATED CONTENT IS CORRECTED DURING MIGRATION — not ported verbatim. Porting it as-is regenerates the exact defect this task exists to remove. Two known instances: (a) line 3's issue, already recorded on this task; (b) PROJECT_PLAN.md:90, the Stage B B.10 row, which cites DEV.38 for a Day 8 seed cross-tenant dealer bug whose entry was never written (F.72, DEV.128) — the generated header and Stage B content must carry the CORRECTED citation. VERIFICATION, corrected after `verifier` showed the first wording was probably unsatisfiable: `pnpm check:ids` must pass against the generated file, and the DEV.38 entry for PROJECT_PLAN.md in scripts/id-reference-allowlist.json must be CONVERTED from kind: deferred-fix to kind: deliberate-mention — NOT deleted. Deleting it fails, because the entry is file-scoped and covers three sites, not one: line 90 is the wrong citation this task fixes, but lines 285 and 292 are generated from F.63's and F.72's own notes, which name DEV.38 in order to say it is missing. Those two are legitimate deliberate mentions and would become newly dangling the moment the entry disappeared. Converting in place counts as satisfying 'no new allowlist entries'; deleting and re-adding does not. The original wording would have walked this task into a small replay of the DEV.112 shape — a criterion that cannot be met — which is exactly what it was written to avoid. WHY THIS TASK AND NOT AN OVERRULE, in the operator's words: 'DEV.112's overrule was justified on unsatisfiability — one commit in history had to fail, and no rule change could avoid it. This is avoidable, the fix is next, and the wrong citation is inert meanwhile. Spending an overrule here would establish that two checks in tension is grounds for bypass, which is exactly the erosion DEV.112 defended against.' The tension is between the verifier's Stage A-E byte-identical check and its dangling-reference check; making PROJECT_PLAN.md fully generated dissolves it rather than trading one check off against the other.

tasks.task: Harden `plan-keeper` against any git state mutation, and fix the main-thread race that triggered one
tasks.notes: Opened by DEV.114. WHAT HAPPENED: the main thread invoked `plan-keeper`, then committed the resulting working-tree changes BEFORE the agent had reported. The agent, still running, found a commit it had not made, correctly judged it inconsistent with its own prohibition on committing, and ran `git reset HEAD~1` to undo it. The commit vanished; the edits survived unstaged; the work was re-committed afterwards. No data was lost. TWO SEPARATE FIXES, and the second matters more than the first. (1) THE RACE, main-thread side: never commit a subagent's output until that subagent has reported. This is a workflow rule and belongs in docs/BUILD_PROMPT_TEMPLATE.md alongside the C7a ordering rule added the same day — the same class of defect, an ordering assumption held in someone's head rather than written down. (2) THE REMIT GAP, agent side: `plan-keeper`'s hard limits enumerate `git add`, `git commit`, `git push`, and creating a branch or PR. `git reset` is not on that list, and the enumeration is exactly what let this through. Replace the list with a blanket prohibition on ANY git state mutation — reset, checkout, revert, stash, cherry-pick, branch -f, rebase — and add the standing instruction: if you find a commit you did not make, REPORT IT and stop; never repair it. An agent whose remit is 'edit one JSON file' must not be able to move HEAD on any reasoning, including correct reasoning, and its reasoning here WAS correct, which is what makes the gap worth closing rather than excusing. RELATED OBSERVATION from the same invocation, bearing on how much to trust an unreviewed agent: the safety classifier was reported unavailable for it, so its output went unreviewed. The main thread verified the JSON independently before re-committing (63 tasks, F.52 still complete with completedDate 2026-09-10, no duplicate ids, no invalid statuses, diff confined to the two lines of the notes field) and the edit was clean. Verifying because a guard reported itself absent is the right order of operations and should be the documented habit. OPERATOR DIRECTION, Day 24 follow-up — SUPERSEDES the 'replace the list with a blanket prohibition' wording above on the mechanism, though not on the intent: implement an ALLOW-LIST of permitted git operations, not a deny-list of remembered prohibited ones. A prohibition list will always have gaps — `git reset` was missing from exactly such a list and that gap is the whole incident. State positively what `plan-keeper` may run (read-only inspection: `git status`, `git diff`, `git log`, `git show`, `git ls-files`) and treat everything else as forbidden by default, including commands nobody thought to name. The same reasoning applies to the other agents' prompts, which all carry enumerated prohibitions — worth sweeping while in there, though only `plan-keeper` has a write tool and therefore the real blast radius.

tasks.task: `grep` returns silent false negatives in the devcontainer — audit the negative-existence claims that depend on it
tasks.notes: Opened by DEV.115, found by `verifier` while re-deriving its own evidence. THE FAULT: on `scripts/sync-project-plan.ts`, `grep` returned exit 1 with NO OUTPUT for strings demonstrably present in the file — including `MARKER_START` and `Changelog` — while `sed` and `node` read the same content correctly. It worked normally on other paths (PROJECT_PLAN.md, DEVIATIONS.md, scripts/sync-project-plan.test.ts). So it fails SILENTLY AND SELECTIVELY, on some paths and not others, with no error and no diagnostic. WHY THIS IS THE WORST FAILURE MODE FOR THIS PROJECT: a large share of Stage F's conclusions are negative existence claims derived from a clean grep — 'no globalSetup anywhere', 'zero restart markers across four CI runs', 'Grep absent from the toolset', 'no ## Changelog in main'. A tool that silently reports 'not found' for content that is present can manufacture any of those, and nothing in the output distinguishes a true negative from a broken read. WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN TO SURVIVE, corroborated by non-grep means: absence of recompiles during the test phase (confirmed by `Compiled /` counts read two ways in CI logs AND by the measured runtime drop 18.8min -> 9.3min); the agent tool-grant mismatches (confirmed by agents enumerating their own function schemas, not by grep); the changelog's absence from main (confirmed by `node` line counts). NOT DIAGNOSED and deliberately not guessed: no cause is claimed. A binary or locale issue, a file-encoding interaction and a sandbox filesystem quirk were all considered and NONE was investigated. Do not write a cause into this task without reproducing it. OPERATIONAL RULE to adopt meanwhile, and the cheapest part of this task: do not accept a negative grep result on its own as proof of absence — confirm with `node`, `sed`, or `git grep`. That belongs in docs/RUNBOOKS.md and in the read-only agents' prompts, several of which instruct the agent to 'grep it and quote it'. SMALL RESIDUE found by the same agent via `node` after grep failed on the file: `INSERT_BEFORE_HEADINGS` in scripts/sync-project-plan.ts still lists `'## Changelog'` as an insertion anchor. Dead today — the markers exist, so the creation path never runs — but it is a live reference to a now-banned section that would quietly re-anchor insertion if the section ever returned. Remove it as part of this task. PRIORITY, set by the operator Day 24 follow-up: keep this ABOVE COSMETIC. It is not a tooling annoyance. `code-auditor` and `doc-auditor` both reason from grep as their primary instrument, and a silent false negative there produces a CONFIDENT WRONG ANSWER rather than a visible failure — an agent reports 'DOES NOT EXIST' with file:line evidence for everything it did find, and nothing in its output distinguishes that from a broken read. Every EXISTS/DOES NOT EXIST verdict in the Stage F record inherits this risk. Visible failures are cheap; confidently wrong verdicts get built on. NARROWED since the entry was written: the verifier reproduced the fault and characterised its blast radius — on `scripts/sync-project-plan.ts`, `grep -c MARKER_START` returns exit 1 with no output while `git grep` reports 4 and `node` and `sed` independently count 4; on `PROJECT_PLAN.md`, `DEVIATIONS.md`, `docs/stage-f-tasks.json` and `scripts/sync-project-plan.test.ts` grep and node agree line-for-line. So it is at least file-specific rather than universal, which makes it more dangerous, not less: a tool that is usually right is trusted. `git grep` worked where `grep` did not, which is a candidate mitigation worth testing before any deeper diagnosis. ROOT CAUSE FOUND, Day 24 follow-up — and it is NOT a sandbox fault, NOT selective-by-path mystery, and NOT a grep bug. `scripts/sync-project-plan.ts` CONTAINS A LITERAL NUL BYTE, at offset 9441, line 264, inside the template literal in `outsideMarkers()`: `return \`${plan.slice(0, pos.start)}\0${plan.slice(pos.end + MARKER_END.length)}\``. It is DELIBERATE and documented — the function's own docstring calls it 'a sentinel standing in for the generated content', and comparing outside-markers before and after is how the verifier proves the script touched nothing else. GNU grep treats ANY file containing a NUL byte as BINARY and suppresses matches, which is the entire observed behaviour: exit 1, no output, no warning. PROOF, four instruments on the same file and pattern: `node` counts 4 occurrences of `MARKER_START`; plain `grep -c` exits 1 with no output; `grep -ac` (force text) returns 4; `git grep -c` returns 4; `rg -c` returns 4. `LC_ALL=C` makes no difference, ruling out the locale/multibyte theory. THE BLAST RADIUS IS ONE FILE, and this is the reassuring part: a sweep of every git-tracked file for NUL bytes returns exactly this script plus genuine binaries (2 PDFs, a .docx, 5 PNGs, 2 sample PDFs). Every other text file in the repo greps correctly, which matches the verifier's earlier observation that grep agreed with node on PROJECT_PLAN.md, DEVIATIONS.md and the test file. So NO Stage F conclusion is at risk unless it grepped THIS script — and the audits were about app routes, schemas, CI logs and specs, none of which touch it. THE CONCLUSION THAT MATTERED MOST WAS RE-VERIFIED ANYWAY: see F.6. MITIGATION ALREADY SHIPPED (Day 24 follow-up): the four Bash-holding agents — doc-auditor, ci-investigator, flake-triager — now carry an explicit search-instrument section directing `git grep` first, `rg` second, `node -e` third, and plain `grep` as CORROBORATION ONLY, never the sole basis for a negative, with `-a` if used at all; doc-auditor's Permitted Bash list was updated to match. code-auditor got the opposite note: its dedicated `Grep` tool is RIPGREP-BACKED and was NEVER AFFECTED, it has no Bash so it cannot reach the broken path, and it was verified correct on this very file — so the instruction there is to keep using it and to stop resting any DOES NOT EXIST on a single search. THE REMAINING FIX, one line, NOT YET DONE and needing an operator decision because it touches the script the plan gate depends on: change the sentinel in `outsideMarkers()` from `\0` to any non-NUL improbable value (a printable token, or `\u0001`). Any sentinel works — it is only ever compared against itself, before versus after — and it eliminates the fault at source rather than routing around it. SEQUENCING NOTE: F.37/F.63 is about to rewrite this script wholesale to render the whole document, so the cheapest moment is inside that change, not before it. Also fold in the previously-noted residue: `INSERT_BEFORE_HEADINGS` still lists `'## Changelog'` as an insertion anchor (line 58), dead today but a live reference to a banned section. CORRECTION, same day, caught by `verifier` before the PR opened. THE 'ROOT CAUSE FOUND' PARAGRAPH ABOVE MISATTRIBUTES THE FAILING TOOL. The NUL byte is real and everything said about it holds — offset 9441, line 264, the deliberate sentinel in `outsideMarkers()`, and the blast radius of exactly one tracked source file plus genuine binaries (independently re-confirmed by a sweep of all 666 tracked files: 11 contain a NUL — 4 PDFs, 1 .docx, 5 PNGs, and this script). WHAT IS WRONG IS THE NAME OF THE BROKEN INSTRUMENT. It is NOT GNU grep. In a Claude Code session `grep` is a SHELL FUNCTION SHIM installed by the harness, backed by UGREP (7.8.4 observed, aarch64). That shim is what exits 1 with no output on a NUL-bearing file. Real GNU grep 3.8 at `/usr/bin/grep` handles the same file and pattern CORRECTLY — returns 4, exit 0 — and with `-n` it prints `binary file matches` and still exits 0, i.e. it is honest about what it is doing. Measured, pattern `MARKER_START`, true count 4 per node: bare `grep -c` exit 1 empty; `grep -ac` 4; `/usr/bin/grep -c` 4 exit 0; `git grep -c` 4 with lines; `rg -c` 4 but `rg -n` prints `binary file matches` and lists NO lines without `-a`; `LC_ALL=C` changes nothing. THE SELF-REFUTATION WAS ALREADY IN THE RECORD AND WAS MISSED: the original paragraph noted 'no Binary file matches line' as part of the symptom. That absence was precisely the evidence it was not GNU grep, because GNU grep does print that line. WHY THE MISATTRIBUTION MATTERS RATHER THAN BEING A PEDANTIC FIX: (1) the failure is SESSION-SCOPED to the Claude Code shim, so it DOES NOT EXIST IN CI, which has no shim — describing it as a repo-and-binary property overstates where it applies; (2) a future agent that tests `/usr/bin/grep`, sees the correct count and exit 0, would reasonably conclude the whole warning is stale and discount it; (3) it misdirects remediation toward the NUL byte — which is deliberate, documented and correct — instead of toward instrument choice, which is the thing actually under anyone's control. SECOND DEFECT FIXED IN THE SAME PASS: the agent prompts' step 2 recommended `rg -n`, which does not list lines on a NUL-bearing file. Corrected to `rg -na`. All four agent prompts were rewritten with the correct attribution, the measured comparison table, and explicit warnings that the property is session-scoped and that `/usr/bin/grep` working does not make the guidance stale. The one-line sentinel fix remains the real elimination and remains sequenced into F.37/F.63. Recorded in DEV.118, which corrects DEV.117.

tasks.task: Typst provisioning prerequisites — devcontainer `xz`, pinned release per arch, and cross-arch determinism
tasks.notes: Opened by F.38 Day 25. The Typst spike PASSED on all four blocking questions (docs/TYPST_SPIKE.md), but it surfaced three provisioning prerequisites that have a DEADLINE — Day 27 cutover — and no owner until now. A deadline recorded only in a spike document is how it gets missed. (1) THE DEVCONTAINER CANNOT UNPACK A TYPST RELEASE. `xz` is not installed, and neither is `sudo`, `cargo`, `7z` or `bsdtar`; Typst ships Linux builds only as `.tar.xz`. The spike got the binary by pulling a pure-JS xz decoder from npm into /tmp — fine for a throwaway, not a provisioning story, and deliberately NOT vendored: `package.json` and the lockfile are unchanged and no decoder or binary was committed. FIX: add `xz-utils` to `.devcontainer/Dockerfile`, which today contains no xz at all (its only `xz` match is `tar -xz`, gzip, for doctl). One line. (2) PIN THE DISTRIBUTION CHANNEL, and check this before anyone proposes the obvious one: the npm `typst` package has exactly the right shape — per-platform optionalDependencies `@typst-community/typst-linux-arm64`, `-linux-x64` — but it is ABANDONED: latest `0.10.0-8`, last published 2023-12-18, five minor versions behind 0.15.1, and community-maintained rather than official. Use the official GitHub release, pinned by tag AND checksum, per arch. Both Linux arches ship from the same tag (`aarch64-unknown-linux-musl`, `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl`), both statically linked — `ldd` reports 'not a dynamic executable' — which is why this is NOT a repeat of DEV.89: that was one x86-64-only binary that could not run on arm64, whereas here the divergence axis is handled rather than traded. Per environment: devcontainer arm64 needs (1) first; GitHub runners have `xz` in `ubuntu-latest` so `tar -xJf` works, and the binary should be cached by version exactly as the Playwright browser cache already is; DO workers get the static binary in the image, replacing a Chromium install, so the layer shrinks substantially and the custom Dockerfile that ADR-013 justifies only by Chromium may stop being necessary. (3) CROSS-ARCH BYTE DETERMINISM IS UNTESTED AND IS A DAY 27 BLOCKER IF IT FAILS. The spike proved determinism on arm64 only: with `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` pinned, two renders are byte-identical including the 500-serial document; unpinned they differ in 88 metadata bytes (ModDate/CreationDate, XMP dates, DocumentID, trailer /ID). What was NOT tested is whether arm64 and x86-64 produce the SAME bytes for the same input. That matters concretely: references are captured in the devcontainer (arm64) and CI snapshot tests would run on x86-64 runners, so if the two disagree, every snapshot test fails on day one. Test this BEFORE Day 27 writes snapshot tests, not after. RELATED, and the reason snapshot tests need care regardless: the `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` pin is mandatory, not optional — without it output changes every render and a snapshot test can never pass. ITEM (3) ANSWERED — CROSS-ARCH DETERMINISM HOLDS, and it is now a standing CI check rather than a one-off measurement. Typst output is BYTE-IDENTICAL across arm64 and x86-64 with `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` pinned. Evidence: fixture rendered on the arm64 devcontainer hashes to `06713a310aa01b092a8c5e4d067aa3050123fc03b4d87a2c831c1e3048a404d5` at 76,699 bytes; the `typst-determinism` job re-rendered the same fixture on an x86-64 GitHub runner and produced the SAME hash and the SAME byte count, reported as `MATCH` in 6 seconds. Also verified: one distinct hash across three consecutive arm64 renders. The fixture is deliberately non-trivial (2 pages, 300 unique serials, 3 rupee glyphs, a table header repeating across a page break) because a minimal document could be byte-stable while a realistic one is not. Lives at `apps/workers/scripts/typst-determinism/` with the job in `.github/workflows/verify.yml`. WHAT THIS CLOSES: the risk was that references captured in the arm64 devcontainer could never match x86-64 CI renders, in which case every snapshot test fails on its first run with no useful signal and the remedy is that REFERENCES MUST BE PRODUCED IN CI rather than locally — a change to Day 25's output, not Day 27's. That risk is closed; local capture is sound. STILL NOT COVERED, by design: determinism across Typst VERSIONS (a version bump is expected to change the hash — re-record from arm64, never from the CI side, which would make the check tautological), and determinism of the real templates, which do not exist yet. NEW REQUIREMENT, OPERATOR-SET — THE PIN BELONGS TO THE RENDERER, NOT THE TEST HARNESS. `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` must be set by the production render path itself, not only by tests. The reasoning is that if it is set only in the test harness then production renders are NON-DETERMINISTIC and the snapshot proves a property the real pipeline does not have — the test would be green while the thing it claims to protect is untrue. Concretely, when Day 27 replaces the `render-pdf` consumer: the renderer must pin the timestamp on every invocation, deterministically and from the document's own data rather than from wall-clock time. The obvious candidate is the document's creation timestamp (`generated_documents.created_at`, or the source document's own date), which makes a re-render of the same document reproduce the same bytes — the property snapshot tests and any future document-integrity check actually need. Do NOT leave it to an environment variable that CI happens to set: an env var absent in production is exactly the shape of this defect. Write the chosen source of the timestamp into the ADR that supersedes ADR-013, because it is a correctness property of the renderer and not a test detail. FOLDED IN FROM DAY 25 FOLLOW-UP AND CONFIRMED BY DAY 26: (4) THE STANDING DETERMINISM CHECK MUST RENDER A REAL DOCUMENT, NOT A SYNTHETIC FIXTURE. The `typst-determinism` CI job compiles apps/workers/scripts/typst-determinism/fixture.typ, which has no timestamp in it at all — so it could not have caught the defect Day 26 found, where `generatedAt: new Date()` in the shared loaders made every render of a real document differ from the last. Day 26 proved determinism on all 14 real documents (14/14 byte-identical across two runs), and that is the property the standing check must hold, not a fixture's. When the renderer moves in-process at Day 27, point the check at a real document rendered through the production path and keep the fixture only as a fast smoke test. (5) `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` IS PINNED INSIDE THE RENDER SCRIPT, NOT SUPPLIED BY THE ENVIRONMENT — the production renderer must own it the same way; a CI-supplied env var is not a guarantee that survives a deploy. CLOSED BY DAY 27. (1) The devcontainer xz blocker is fixed at the image: .devcontainer/Dockerfile now installs xz-utils and puts ~/.local/bin on PATH, so `pnpm typst:install` works from the next container rebuild. (2) Provisioning is scripts/install-typst.mjs — pinned version AND a per-architecture sha256, verified before install, with the same version pinned in apps/workers/Dockerfile and .github/workflows/verify.yml; `pnpm typst:check` fails a job whose resolved binary is a different version. The abandoned npm wrapper is not used and there is deliberately no download-on-demand at render time. (3) Cross-arch determinism now runs ON A REAL DOCUMENT: the typst-determinism job seeds a database and renders the 500-serial dispatch note, comparing sha256 against a hash recorded on arm64. The synthetic fixture is deleted — it had no timestamp in it, so it could not have caught the generatedAt defect Day 26 actually found while the fixture sat green. (4) SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH is set by the RENDERER from the document's own instant (src/pdf/typst.ts), not by a harness or an env var, so the snapshots prove a property production actually has.

tasks.task: critical-path e2e: an 800ms sleep races the stage-transition commit, and that is the flake's actual cause
tasks.notes: Found by flake-triager during F.67 Part 2, while ruling the seed-clock pin OUT as the cause of a flaky run. RULED OUT FIRST, so nobody re-investigates it: the pipeline board is not date-sensitive. apps/web/lib/queries/deals.ts:103 orders by desc(hot), desc(lastActivityAt) — DESCENDING, so a freshly created deal has the maximum last_activity_at and sits toward the TOP of its column; pinning seeded rows into the past moves a new card toward view, not away from it. listDealsByStage has no LIMIT, no OFFSET and no pagination; pipeline-board.tsx:172 maps every card with no virtualiser and droppable-column.tsx clips nothing vertically; and pin-created-at.ts rewrites only created_at/updated_at, which the board does not sort on. The one date filter that exists, deals.ts:73 opts.activeSince, has no caller anywhere in the repo. THE ACTUAL CAUSE: critical-path.spec.ts's moveDealTo does `await page.waitForTimeout(800)` and then `page.goto('/pipeline')`. commitMove fires transitionDealStage inside startTransition, so the navigation aborts the client's read of that response while the server keeps committing. The reloaded page is force-dynamic and server-rendered, so when its SSR query runs before the action's transaction commits, the board renders the card in the OLD column — and the 15s toBeVisible then retries against a static DOM that will never change, burning the full budget. Evidence from the one observed failure: the deal existed in the database at the asserted stage (deal_stage_history shows verbal_commit → po_pending committed at 13:21:37.816Z) while the assertion reported 'element(s) not found', which is the exists-but-not-rendered case rather than a state bug; the failing attempt took 16.9s between those two transitions against 3.6–4.3s in five healthy runs. FIX SHAPE, not yet decided: wait for the server's own signal rather than sleeping — the transition's response, or a visible post-commit change — instead of a fixed 800ms. DO NOT 'fix' this by raising the 15s timeout: the timeout is the symptom and the sleep is the cause, and the standing rule is that no spec gets a longer timeout to hide a race. NOT REPRODUCED in isolation: 5/5 passes standalone with a freshly booted dev server and globalSetup's warm-up. It failed at the END of a full pnpm verify, against a dev server that had already compiled and evicted ~40 routes, which is the condition that makes the race lose.

tasks.task: verify.yml runs on PRs into main ONLY, so a stacked PR merges with zero CI — widen the trigger to any branch
tasks.notes: Opened by DEV.123; scope settled by DEV.124 after measurement. THE FAULT: .github/workflows/verify.yml triggers on `pull_request: branches: [main]`, so a pull request targeting any other branch runs NO CI at all — not a failure, not a skip, no checks exist. `gh pr checks <n>` reports 'no checks reported', which reads like a queue that has not started rather than a gate that is absent. THE FIX, DECIDED: widen `branches:` so pull requests into any branch run the suite. Do NOT instead add `edited` to `types:`. Widening checks the code BEFORE it enters the intermediate branch, which is where the unchecked merge actually happens; `edited` would only check it after it had been carried upward, and fires on every title and body edit besides. MEASURED, so the cost objection can be weighed rather than assumed: across all 21 pull requests in the repository's history, exactly THREE have ever targeted a non-main base — #16, #17, and #20, the last being a throwaway probe opened to settle this question. So two genuine occurrences in nineteen real PRs. At roughly 9-10 minutes for the e2e job, widening the trigger would have cost about twenty minutes of additional CI across the entire project to date. CONCURRENCY: THE COLLISION DOES NOT EXIST, and the earlier worry that two PRs sharing a head ref could cancel each other was wrong. The group is `${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}`, and on a pull_request event `github.ref` is `refs/pull/<PR number>/merge`, NOT the head branch — confirmed empirically from run 34701098445's log, where actions/checkout runs `git checkout --progress --force refs/remotes/pull/19/merge`. The group is therefore already unique per PR number, so two PRs sharing a head branch land in different groups and neither cancels the other. LEAVE `concurrency` EXACTLY AS IT IS; changing it to key on the PR number would only re-implement what github.ref already provides. The one real consequence of widening is duplicated work rather than cancellation: a head branch with two open PRs (one into main, one into another branch) runs the suite twice per push. Rare, and acceptable. STILL TO CHECK WHEN IMPLEMENTING: the `push: branches: [main]` trigger is deliberately a RECORD and not a gate — main has already begun deploying by the time it runs — so leave it alone; and confirm the ruleset's required status checks still match the job names afterwards, because branch protection matches on job name and a rename silently removes a required check. WHAT THIS TASK DOES NOT COVER: the retargeting half of DEV.123. That is closed by the repository's 'Automatically delete head branches' setting, which was OFF during the trap and is now on — verified by probe PR #20, which retargeted from a deleted base branch to main when PR #19 merged. But #20 arrived at main with ZERO CHECKS, which is precisely why this task survives that setting rather than being closed by it. DO NOT close this by adding a convention asking people not to stack PRs — R22 already carries that, and the point here is the structural half that does not depend on anyone remembering.

tasks.task: A successful PDF render logs nothing, so 'did it render?' cannot be answered from logs
tasks.notes: Found on 2026-09-14 while trying to confirm the first production render after the Typst cutover. A gap in observability, not in the renderer. THE FAULT, verified in code: apps/workers/src/jobs/render-pdf.ts contains ZERO logger calls — neither runRenderPdf nor handleRenderPdfJob logs anything on success — and nothing else on the path does either: the same grep over apps/workers/src/pdf/, apps/web/lib/pdf/render-request.ts and apps/web/lib/actions/quotations/generate-pdf.ts is empty. So a completed render is indistinguishable from one that never happened. THE FIX IS ALREADY HALF-BUILT, which is the part worth knowing: `pdf.generated` is ALREADY DECLARED in the trackEvent contract on both sides — apps/workers/src/observability/event-types.ts:52 and apps/web/lib/observability/event-types.ts:52, typed as { documentId: string; documentType: string } — and it is EMITTED NOWHERE. The only reference in application code outside the two declarations is a web test (apps/web/lib/observability/events.test.ts:67); the name also appears in BUILD_PROMPTS.md:4916, in the Day 17 contract that declared it. This is the placeholder pattern: a declared value with nothing writing it is not an implementation. So the work is to emit an event the contract already reserves, matching how email/handler.ts:143 emits `email.sent`, rather than to design new telemetry — and trackEvent ships to Axiom and logs via pino as a side effect, so the record outlives DO's run-log buffer. Consider widening the payload to carry generatedDocumentId, sizeBytes and duration_ms; keep tenant data to ids only, per docs/LOGGING.md's eight-stream surface. pdf-cleanup IS ALREADY INSTRUMENTED and is the model to copy, not a second gap — jobs/pdf-cleanup.ts:42 logs 'pdf-cleanup sweep complete' with its result, and jobs/validity-expiry.ts:65 does the same; the first version of this task wrongly listed pdf-cleanup as also missing telemetry, and someone acting on that would have 'fixed' a job that was already correct. PRECISION ABOUT WHICH SURFACE REPORTS WHAT, because it is the whole question: apps/workers/src/index.ts makes exactly TWO logger calls, :71 on start and :94 on start failure. captureJobError in observability/sentry.ts is Sentry.captureException and does NOT reach the log stream at all. The third failure log is queue/boss.ts:68 ('pg-boss error'), not in index.ts. WHY IT MATTERS MORE NOW than under Chromium: the old path had a warm-up line, recycle logs with reasons, and a cold-start signature, so render activity was visible as a side effect of the browser's lifecycle. Typst has no lifecycle, so that incidental visibility went with the browser. COMPOUNDING FACTOR, observed twice in six hours: DO App Platform's run-log buffer is short and a deploy rotates it. PR #24 (docs only) redeployed both apps at 09:51 UTC, and PR #25 (docs only) redeployed them again at ~16:04 — each time discarding the window containing the render under investigation. SHARPER, AND WORSE, established 2026-09-14 while trying to confirm a second production render: the run log cannot distinguish a SUCCESSFUL render from a FAILED one. Success logs nothing, as recorded above — but failure does not reach the run log either. instrumentJobHandler (observability/sentry.ts:60-78) captures a throwing job to Sentry via captureJobError (sentry.ts:40-47) and rethrows; pg-boss then RETRIES IT TWICE WITH NO BACKOFF — three attempts in total. The exact figure matters for anyone verifying a render by counting Sentry events: retryLimit=5 with retryBackoff is EMAIL_QUEUE_RETRY (queue/boss.ts:19-22), applied at boss.ts:72-73 only when queue === EMAIL_QUEUE. RENDER_PDF_QUEUE is created bare at boss.ts:75 and takes pg-boss 10.4.2's default retry_limit of 2. So expect three captures in rapid succession, not five spread out. The only pg-boss logging is instance.on('error') at queue/boss.ts:67-69, which is an INSTANCE-level handler for pg-boss's own failures, not a per-job one. So a render that throws — for example because the Typst binary is missing in the image — produces an ACTIVE, healthy-looking workers process and a silent run log, and is visible only in Sentry and in the absence of a generated_documents row. That is why the first two attempts to confirm a production render from logs could not succeed in either direction, and it is the strongest argument for emitting the already-declared pdf.generated event: it converts 'no evidence' into 'positive evidence', which is a different thing. When wiring it, emit on the failure path too, or the log still answers only half the question. tasks.notes: Opened by the operator on 2026-09-14 after the pattern cost investigation a second time. THE PATTERN: a value is declared in a contract — an event name, an enum member, a settings key — and nothing ever writes it. It reads as implemented to anyone who greps for it, and is not. This is the placeholder rule the code-auditor agent already states for existence questions ('a declared value with nothing writing it is a placeholder, not an implementation'), but nothing enumerates them, so each is discovered separately at the moment it misleads someone. SCOPE, corrected by `verifier` before this task started: the two instances below are what was KNOWN, not what exists. An enumeration of every trackEvent reference against both event-types.ts files found EIGHT events actually emitted in production — dispatch.created, order.confirmed, quotation.created, quotation.sent, user.logged_in, user.password_changed, email.bounced, email.sent — against 23 declared in each of the two event-types.ts files (mirrors of each other: `diff` reports a single differing line, the header comment on line 13, where each copy names the other as its mirror — the declarations themselves are identical), so FOURTEEN more unemitted events sit behind the two named here (8 emitted + 14 + pdf.generated = 23, which is the arithmetic to check the list against when the sweep runs): tenant.created, dealer.created, product.created, inventory.procurement_created, deal.created, deal.stage_advanced, quotation.accepted, pi.created, pi.confirmed, order.cancelled, payment.recorded, payment.allocated, payment.bounced, dispatch.delivered. Do NOT go in expecting most of them to classify as DELIBERATE RESERVATION — that was this task’s initial guess and there is evidence against it: Day 17 A3.4 (BUILD_PROMPTS.md:4919-4920) instructed "Wire trackEvent calls at the right points", the first of which is "Inside successful Server Actions, after the DB transaction commits but before returning", a general instruction across the contract rather than a per-event reservation. The split between reservation and gap is the finding, not an input. The two known instances, both found while investigating something else, are: (1) `pdf.generated` is declared in the trackEvent contract on BOTH sides — apps/workers/src/observability/event-types.ts:52 and apps/web/lib/observability/event-types.ts:52, typed { documentId: string; documentType: string } — and emitted nowhere; the only other reference in application code is a web test (apps/web/lib/observability/events.test.ts:67), which asserts the call does not throw; the name also appears in BUILD_PROMPTS.md:4916, in the Day 17 contract that declared it. Found during F.73, where it changed the shape of the fix from 'design telemetry' to 'emit the event the contract already reserves'. (2) The 'invoice' member of the generated_documents document-type enum — declared, and nothing produces it. It has been in the pgEnum since f547dd3 (2026-05-15, "feat(pdf): chunk a — puppeteer worker scaffold + storage schema"), i.e. DAY 10, which is consistent with the Day 10 reservation rationale further down this note. It was described as "from Day 19" in the operator message that opened this task, and that attribution stood in this note until 8e735a8; Day 19 (e3e3afe) is the security day whose audit FOUND the tax invoice missing, not where the enum member was declared. THE WORK: enumerate, do not fix. Produce a written list of (a) every event name in both event-types.ts files with no emit site, and (b) every enum value in packages/db/src/schema that nothing writes, each marked as either DELIBERATE RESERVATION (the contract is stable ahead of the feature, which is a legitimate pattern — the generated_documents enum was deliberately declared complete in Day 10 so the queue contract would not churn) or ACCIDENTAL GAP. The deliverable is the list and the classification; wiring anything is separate work. METHOD NOTE: use affirmative enumeration, not grep-for-absence — read both event-types.ts files and the schema enums in full and check each member against its call sites, rather than grepping for names and trusting empty results. The verdicts are negative-existence claims, which is exactly the shape DEV.115/DEV.118 recorded a silently-failing instrument for.
